presentingComplaint: 3 weeks of low-grade evening fever, worsening headache, and increasing confusion for 4 days
history: A 34-year-old woman from a TB-endemic region presents with a 3-week history of low-grade, evening-predominant fever, drenching night sweats, and unintentional weight loss of approximately 4 kg. Over the past 10 days she has developed a dull, gradually worsening holocranial headache with associated photophobia and intermittent vomiting. For the last 4 days her family has noted progressive behavioral change, apathy, and difficulty recognizing family members, with one witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure earlier today. There is no history of head trauma. She reports no cough, but her husband was treated for pulmonary TB 8 months ago and the couple lives in the same household. No history of diabetes, HIV testing has never been done, and she is not on any immunosuppressive medication.
examination: Drowsy but rousable, oriented to person only, GCS 12/15 (E3V3M6). Neck stiffness present with positive Kernig sign. Photophobia present. Cranial nerve exam reveals a subtle right partial ptosis with sluggishly reactive pupil suggestive of early third/sixth nerve involvement; fundoscopy shows bilateral early papilledema without frank choroidal tubercles visualized. No focal limb weakness at present but reflexes are brisk bilaterally with equivocal plantars. No skin rash, no lymphadenopathy, chest clear to auscultation, no hepatosplenomegaly.

labs.csf_appearance: clear, mildly turbid, cobweb clot on standing

imaging: Contrast MRI brain: basal exudates thickening the suprasellar and interpeduncular cisterns with leptomeningeal enhancement; mild communicating hydrocephalus; no discrete ring-enhancing tuberculoma seen but small punctate enhancing foci in basal ganglia region suspicious for early tuberculomas
Chest X-ray: no active parenchymal infiltrate; old fibrotic scarring at right apex, no cavitation
microbiology: CSF AFB smear negative (expected low sensitivity, does not exclude TBM)
CSF mycobacterial culture (MGIT) sent, result pending (weeks)
Blood cultures sent, no growth at 48h
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e — Tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis infections) and CNS infections chapters
WHO Consolidated Guidelines on Tuberculosis — Module 1: Prevention, and Guidelines for management of drug-susceptible TB 2022
IDSA/ATS/CDC/ERS Clinical Practice Guidelines: Treatment of Drug-Susceptible Tuberculosis 2016
stewardship: Empirical anti-tuberculous therapy should be started promptly on clinical suspicion without waiting for microbiological confirmation, given the high morbidity/mortality of delayed treatment: standard four-drug intensive phase (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for 2 months followed by isoniazid and rifampicin continuation phase, extended to a total of 9-12 months for CNS disease per guideline recommendation; adjunctive corticosteroids (dexamethasone or prednisolone with taper) are recommended for all HIV-negative patients with TBM to reduce mortality and neurological sequelae; evaluate for hydrocephalus requiring neurosurgical CSF diversion.
contraindications: Confirm baseline liver function before starting isoniazid/rifampicin/pyrazinamide given hepatotoxicity risk
Screen for pregnancy status and HIV status before finalizing regimen and steroid dosing decisions
Ethambutol dose adjustment and visual acuity/color vision baseline testing needed
Avoid delaying empirical anti-TB therapy pending culture confirmation, as this worsens neurological outcome
edgeCases: CSF AFB smear and even GeneXpert can be negative in a substantial proportion of TBM cases (paucibacillary CSF); diagnosis often remains 'probable' based on clinico-radiological-CSF criteria (e.g., Thwaites/consensus TBM diagnostic criteria/Lancet uniform case definition) pending culture
Low CSF ADA (14 U/L) does not exclude TBM as sensitivity/specificity of ADA is imperfect and cutoffs vary by lab
HIV status unknown — if HIV-positive, corticosteroid benefit and drug interactions (rifampicin with antiretrovirals) require reassessment
Hyponatremia may reflect SIADH or cerebral salt wasting, both recognized complications of TBM, and requires careful fluid/sodium management
Communicating hydrocephalus may progress and require urgent neurosurgical CSF diversion (VP shunt or external ventricular drain) independent of antimicrobial therapy
expectedMaiK: MaiK should flag subacute fever/headache/altered sensorium with basal meningeal enhancement, hydrocephalus, and lymphocyte-predominant CSF with low glucose/high protein as high pre-test probability for tuberculous meningitis in a TB-endemic/contact setting, recommending immediate empirical anti-TB therapy plus adjunctive corticosteroids without awaiting culture confirmation, while flagging need for HIV testing and neurosurgical review for hydrocephalus.
